utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. We have a delayed start because of another commitment of myself, and we will have an extended sitting tomorrow so that there is no loss of court time. The next witness should be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution has, I assume, some questions for you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon, General Tolimir, my learned colleagues. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state and spell your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Okay. My name is Louis Fortin, L-o-u-i-s F-o-r-t-i-n, Lieutenant-Colonel in the Canadian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recall testifying over the course of two days in this courtroom back in November of 2007?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to read all of your testimony in that case, the Popovic case, recently?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you attest, sir, before this Trial Chamber that the transcripts which you read fairly and accurately reflect what you said here during that trial?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you further attest, sir, that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked back in November of 2007, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Of course. I would make sure to do my best that they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P586 and P587, Colonel Fortin's Popovic testimony, the latter exhibit being the public version, the former under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, I would like to read a summary of Colonel Fortin's testimony in the Popovic case. At the time he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you do that, I should indicate for the record these are the P numbers 586 under seal and P587. Sorry for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At the time he testified in the Popovic case, Colonel Fortin had served for 31 years in the Canadian Forces in various staff, instructor, and command positions. In May 1995 he held the rank of major and began a year-long tour of duty in Bosnia, serving as the military assistant to General Herve Gobillard, the commander of Sector Sarajevo which was headquartered in the PTT building in Sarajevo. Colonel Fortin accompanied General Gobillard to meetings with political and military personnel of the various factions or with other UN personnel. He took notes, shared advice with Gobillard, and discussed the situation with him regularly. He was also a link to the headquarters staff and would pass information he gathered from meetings he attended and in turn pass on situation reports from the staff to Gobillard. The fact that Colonel Fortin speaks French and English made it easier to work with Gobillard and the largely French Sector Sarajevo headquarters staff, as well as with the mostly English-speaking staff of the superior command at UNPROFOR BiH command headquarters, also located in Sarajevo. Colonel Fortin maintained a list of politicians and senior military personnel from the warring factions. The two or three names which came to his mind quickest from the VRS high command were Generals Mladic, Tolimir, and Dragomir Milosevic, in addition to Generals Miletic, Gvero, and Krstic. Sector Sarajevo corresponded to the corps level in the VRS. BiH command, Colonel Fortin's then-superior command, normally interacted with the senior officers such as Mladic, Tolimir, Miletic, and Gvero. Between approximately 8 July and 11 July 1995, General Gobillard was acting BiH commander in General Rupert Smith's absence. Consequently, Colonel Fortin spent most of his time during this period with Gobillard at BiH command headquarters instead of the Sector Sarajevo headquarters. Key officers present during this period at BiH command included General Nicolai and Lieutenant-Colonel Jim Baxter. Colonel Fortin and these officers spent most of their time during this period determining what was happening on the ground in Srebrenica. Information was passing from Dutch peacekeepers in Srebrenica to their command and up to the BiH command in Sarajevo. They also received reports from British personnel in the enclave who were reporting directly to BiH command, as well as reports from the Bosnian government. Generals Nicolai and Gobillard also had telephone conversations with Generals Tolimir and Gvero during this time. The Dutch peacekeepers and British personnel in the enclave were telling UNPROFOR to do something because they were attacked by the VRS, whereas Tolimir and Gvero were telling them that they were not attacking; that the Bosnians were attacking; that the VRS was not attacking UNPROFOR or the civilians; that the Bosnians were using stolen UN APCs; and that they would confirm what was happening on the ground and call UNPROFOR back 30 minutes later. These were delaying tactics which created confusion and slowed the decision to authorise close air support and in the meantime allowed the VRS to keep attacking and advance further, making the use of close air support even more difficult. It was clear to Colonel Fortin that they were just trying to delay so that they could complete the plan. Colonel Fortin testified about his notes of a conversation between Generals Gvero and Gobillard on 11 July at 1810 hours as well as an intercept of that conversation. By this time UNPROFOR had suspended close air support because the VRS had threatened to kill some captured Dutch soldiers if close air support continued. The Serbs also threatened to shell the UN Potocari compound with all the civilians and peacekeepers in it if close air support continued. Colonel Fortin was also shown numerous passages from a journal he compiled upon his return from his tour, which was made up of his contemporaneous handwritten notes interspersed with cut and pasted reports he had written at the time, in 1995. He also testified about reports concerning problems with Ukrainian peacekeepers, including that those in Zepa were selling their fuel to the Serbs. Around 26 July 1995, General Gobillard sent Colonel Fortin to Zepa to be his eyes and ears. UNPROFOR already had information that suggested that thousands of Bosnian males had disappeared and been killed. The VRS stopped the witness at a check-point in Rogatica for 18 hours. By the time he arrived there, the transportations had already begun. When he finally passed from Rogatica to check-point 2 on the top of the hill, he saw trucks taking the Bosnian civilians up out of Zepa village and described the scene as he watched mothers and their children being forcibly removed from their homes. He described a meeting on 27 July in which Mr. Torlak and two Muslim representatives met with General Mladic, who was trying to get them to sign an agreement and made veiled threats. General Smith then arrived and told the Muslims not to sign because Mladic's agreement contained guarantees which could not be met and aspects, such as conditions of prisoner exchange, which needed to be agreed at a much higher level. Finally, Colonel Fortin spent the night of 27 July in the Ukrainian compound down in the Zepa village and described a meeting he had in the afternoon of 28 July 1995 at check-point 2 between Generals Tolimir and Gobillard, who had travelled to Zepa that day, meaning General Gobillard had travelled to Zepa that day. Gobillard confronted Tolimir about several issues, including approximately 36 Muslim men who had been removed from the last two convoys in the evening of 27 July; the link between the fate of the Zepa men and the ongoing negotiations at the Sarajevo airport for a global POW exchange agreement; and the report that Avdo Palic was dead. Mr. President, at this time the Prosecution would tender Exhibits P580 to P595 from the Prosecution's exhibit list, and that includes everything on the list, including the two transcripts which have already been admitted, with the exception of the last item on the Prosecution's list which has not been previously shown to Colonel Fortin and I intend to show him that document shortly. But prior to that, I would tender these exhibits which were either admitted through Colonel Fortin's Popovic testimony or were shown to the witness during his testimony but admitted through other witnesses in Popovic, were shown to the witness but not tendered in Popovic. I think that's about all the categories we've got, Mr. President, but they're all being offered as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. The Chamber appreciates this distinction between the different categories of documents. They all will be received, P585 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel, I just have a few additional questions for you today. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how many years in the service you have.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm now just about at 34 years of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber in open session generally what you were doing for the military presently. If we need to go into private to do so, we can certainly do that, but if there's a way to just give the Trial Chamber some idea of what you're up to, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm currently Canada's defence attache to western Africa. I'm a resident in Abidjan, Cote d'Ivoire, but I'm also co-accredited to Senegal, Sierra Leone, Mali, Ghana, Nigeria, and Cameroon, so I travel within a subregion to effect my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. You are the first live UNPROFOR officer that has appeared so far in this trial, I think, with the exception of perhaps a DutchBat soldier who testified. So it may be helpful for you to provide just a little bit of the structure of UNPROFOR as it existed in July of 1995. We threw out some places and terms and commands during the summary, Sector Sarajevo, BiH command. If you could just briefly take us through from top to bottom in July 1995 the various echelons of command within UNPROFOR, starting with the one based in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to point out first that at that time in July 1995, or shortly before, United Nations headquarters decided to change the names of the various missions. So the old terminology, BH command, was still being used as opposed to the new name, which was headquarters UNPROFOR, United Nations Protection Force. But the structure was HQ UNPF in Zagreb where resided the force commander, and he was responsible for the whole UN theatre of operations, which included two missions, a mission in Croatia, which was still ongoing - and I don't remember the exact name of that mission; and a mission in Bosnia which was headquarters -- headquartered in Sarajevo, and that mission's name was UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR was divided in three sectors, Sector South, Sector North-West, and Sector Sarajevo. Sector Sarajevo, where I worked, was under the command of a French general officer who had troops from France, three battalions, but also a battalion each from Ukraine, Russia, and Egypt, and he was responsible for Sarajevo itself, including the airport; a portion of the Igman mountains, which are west of the city; and the enclaves or pockets of Zepa and Gorazde. So that basically was the structure of the mission at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel. Now, going back to the UNPF in Zagreb, I take it that's -- that was the highest echelon of command. And who was the commander that was based in Zagreb, what was his name, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: The commander was a French general officer by the name of Janvier, General Janvier. So in that structure General Rupert Smith, who commanded UNPROFOR, which is the Bosnia mission, reported to Janvier; and General Gobillard, who commanded the Sarajevo sector of UNPROFOR, reported to Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when we refer to BiH command or UNPROFOR command, we're speaking about Rupert Smith's echelon, the command that was located in the residency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your command was located in the PTT building in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just give us some idea of the distance between the two?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, the residency HQ UNPROFOR was centre east of the city and Sector Sarajevo was closer to the airport in the west, I estimate about 4 or 5 kilometres in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during your service as General Gobillard's military assistant, Colonel, how often would you shuttle between those two headquarters in the course of your duties?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, initially -- that is, I got there on May 15th, 1995, and shortly thereafter military action picked up, became quite intense. It never -- it never really slowed down until September. So whenever I was in Sarajevo, I used to go almost every night to headquarters UNPROFOR in addition to the trips that I took accompanying my boss during the day because we often visited General Smith where the two generals exchanged together. So I spent quite a bit of my time at headquarters UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And let's fill in some names and positions as well. You were General Gobillard's military assistant. Who was your counterpart with General Smith, who was his military assistant?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: He was Lieutenant-Colonel Jim Baxter, who was a British officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did General Smith have a Chief of Staff who served directly under him?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, his Chief of Staff was General Nicolai, a Dutch army officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did General Nicolai himself also have somebody who was his deputy or immediate subordinate?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He was responsible for the staff of that headquarters, and his main staff officer was -- the man in charge of operations at that time was a Canadian lieutenant-colonel name -- initially was Colonel MacDonald, but he was shortly after replaced by Colonel Rick Hatton.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you also recall interacting with a Colonel Coiffet?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Coiffet, I don't remember his exact position, but he was a French officer. I believe he was -- he had an established position within the headquarters, headquarters UNPROFOR, but he was also acting as a liaison with headquarters of Sector Sarajevo, which was mostly staffed by French officer and commanded by a French general.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just a couple of additional questions on the structure. When you were speaking about the command to which you were attached, Sector Sarajevo, you described that it had several elements, and I believe you referred to a Ukrainian contingent that was serving as part of Sector Sarajevo or underneath Sector Sarajevo. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what responsibilities the Ukrainian contingent had.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: The Ukrainian contingent was a battalion of about 600 people from memory. It had headquarters in Sarajevo at Tito barracks, which was somewhere in between the two headquarters I was talking about earlier, and in one of its three companies was located at Tito barracks and they had anti-sniping task. They had a few spots in the city assigned to cover sniping coming from the Serb side from those locations. The other two companies were located one in Zepa manning check-points and observation posts around the enclave, and last company, the third one, was doing the same thing in Gorazde, which was the southern-most of the three eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard a lot about the Dutch contingent. You have referred to General Nicolai, for example. And certainly the Trial Chamber's heard about the Dutch Battalion peacekeepers who were located in the Srebrenica enclave. Under which direct command did the Dutch peacekeepers in the Srebrenica enclave fall, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Actually, the -- it was a Dutch Company and the unit it belonged to, the battalion it belonged to, was in Sector North-West, which -- that sector had the responsibility of the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of other definitional questions. You referred in your Popovic testimony here -- there to some General Staff positions by abbreviations, G1, G2, I think at one time your position after leaving your tour was at J9. If you could explain to the Trial Chamber just briefly, what does G1, G2, G3, G4, for example, connote?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Actually, this is a system which we referred to as the continental staff system, I believe we owe it to the Germans, to classify the various functions within the headquarters by a -- the notation such as G for General Staff or J for joint staff at higher levels. So G1, 2, 3, 4, 5 at the headquarters level. Everybody in NATO was using the same terminology. J1 or G1 was personnel, so people working in that branch were looking after personnel matters. G2 was intelligence. G3 operations. G4 logistics. And G5 was civil/military co-operation and looking after activities that were for the benefit of the populations in the areas we were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And because we may be seeing this in other documents or from other witnesses later, sir, at lower-level commands were the designations the same in terms of the G or was there another letter which would correspond to those respective positions?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, not every army was using the system at the lower level. For example, in the Canadian Army at battalion level we were using the old British system, which is -- instead of having a G1, we could them the adjutant, the unit adjutant. He was responsible for personnel issues. In the American army they were using the S system, S1, 2, 3, 4, 5, which basically correspond to the same functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that, Colonel. In your Popovic testimony you referred to General Tolimir and I believe some other VRS officers as belonging to the army level of command as opposed to, for example, the corps level of command. When you use that term, "army level," can you specify what you were referring to in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: It's the top level of command within the VRS, as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And have you heard that referred to as the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, yes. We would use that term as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: On a separate issue, Colonel, you testified about a conversation for which you were present between a representative of the Muslim community in Zepa on or about the 15th of July, 1995, a man whose name you recalled as either Horlak or Torlak. Do you recall testifying about hearing a particular conversation concerning that individual or involving that individual, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, and I have to specify, I was present for the conversation but I was not in Zepa. The conversation was through the Ukrainian radio. They had link between their company headquarters and Zepa, and their detachment at the sector headquarters in Sarajevo where Ukrainian officers in the operation zone were manning a radio that was compatible with the system that they had deployed in Zepa. So those -- that equipment was used for -- by Mr. Torlak to talk back.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just talk about that for a couple more moments. You had occasion to go down into the village of Zepa, as you testified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, but it was later -- you mentioned this conversation on the 15th of July. I went there on the 26th and I think I only went down to the village on the evening of the 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you went down there that approximately two weeks later after that conversation, did you yourself have an opportunity to observe the communications equipment that Mr. Torlak was using to communicate to Sarajevo which you overheard in the operations room in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, when we were there -- when I arrived, the Ukrainians were using still that equipment to report back to sector headquarters in Sarajevo; and the deputy sector commander from Ukraine, Colonel Verhoglyad met me when I arrived there and gave me a tour of the facilities. So I was able to see their communication equipment which was in fact in a radio van, a military vehicle which housed communication equipment in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you just describe what that equipment was just briefly.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, it was I would say, older HF-type radios. HF is a type of frequency, it's short wave, not quite like the amateur radio systems that many of us know about, but still shorter waves allow to talk through longer distances. So they were able to talk back to sector headquarters with that equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just physically, can you describe where this Ukrainian company command post was located in the Zepa village, just describe for the Trial Chamber how it was situated?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I believe it was a school and there were two buildings perpendicular to one another, rectangular buildings, and in the space in between there was that communication van as well as one of their armoured personnel carriers, it was a BTR-70 that was providing protection for that communication equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what's the terrain like right in that area, the village of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, it's surrounded by a very steep -- not hills, but it's kind of a -- in French we say "une cuvette" or a bowl with very steep sides and that's where the village was located, down a -- to access the village from the top, there was a single-lane road, one -- a dirt road attached to the -- basically to the flank of that cliff, and only one vehicle could go up and down at a time. And if I remember correctly, that road was slightly longer than a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based upon your experience serving in Sector Sarajevo, how frequently would that Ukrainian company based down in that -- the bottom of that "cuvette" communicate via that radio with its command in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, there was a procedure in place of course with all subunits of every level reporting regularly to the next level up. So in the case of the company, the Ukrainian company, reporting back to sector headquarters, it was at a minimum on a daily basis. But it could have been more. I don't remember for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just help us out with one thing, Colonel. You mention the name of the Ukrainian officer Verugad or something to that effect. If you could spell it for the record so we have it clearly in the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Okay, if I remember it's pronounced Verhoglyad, but it's spelled V-e-r-h-o-g-l-y-a-d. Yeah, that looks right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, I want to show you a document that you didn't see during the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have P00596 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you'll shortly see a document popping up on your computer screen. We have here an UNPROFOR inter-office memorandum. Its date is 13 July 1995. The subject is report of a meeting held in Lukavica between Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic and MA, military assistant, to DSCU and UKRBAT LO - 13 July afternoon. Two questions: One, do you recognise what this is? And two, if you do, can you define for us or explain some of these acronyms here in the subject line?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: All right. This is something that I wrote based on information given to me by someone else, and I was writing to my boss, General Gobillard, and a number of officers under his command to inform them of that information. The officer who attended the meeting were Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic is the Serb liaison officer of the 1st Corps, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which was the Serb military outfit that surrounded Sarajevo, so he was a regular contact, Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic. The next one, the MA to DSCU is the military assistant to the deputy sector commander Ukrain, so Colonel Verhoglyad's military assistant, his name was Captain Andre Schumak. And the UKRBAT LO is the Ukrainian Battalion liaison officer that they had stationed or going regularly to meet with Colonel Indjic who attended that meeting with the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what or where is Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, Lukavica is just to the south-west of Sarajevo, not very far from PTT building where we were located, but it's on the Serb side and it was a former military barrack of the Yugoslav Army that the Serbs were using, the VRS was using.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the second page in English, please, and this is going to be the third page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to focus your attention on paragraphs 7, 8, and 9. If you would, sir, just take a moment or two to read those three paragraphs. And when you've done so I would ask you just to explain to the Trial Chamber where this information was coming from exactly and how it was arriving to you, through whom it arrived to get to you, and from where. And let's start with paragraph 7. Can you tell us in that paragraph who was the source of this information and what does this reflect? We can all read what it says, but if you could just tell us where this information is coming from.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, the information is coming from Indjic, the VRS liaison officer at Lukavica. The one that the two Ukrainian officers went to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this information in paragraph 7 is being relayed to you through the officer Schumak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. One of the two Ukrainian officers who attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we see a heading between these two paragraphs referring to the commanding officer of the Ukrainian Battalion joining the meeting. Can you just explain what's happening here, please, and where this information is coming from.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: In fact, when Captain Schumak was reporting this to me during the course of doing that, that report, the CO of the Ukrainian Battalion showed up. The CO, commanding officer, of the battalion is located in Sarajevo at Tito barracks as I mentioned earlier, but he also had contact with his company in Zepa. So he got the information from them and he came to relay it to probably Colonel Verhoglyad, but we were there so he passed it on to me and Captain Schumak who were in the process of drafting that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So if we look at paragraph 8 here, Colonel, where it says: "The commanding officer of the Rogatica Brigade accompanied by General Tolimir and the local Bosnian authorities met at Ukrainian check-point 2 at 1200 hours today ..." What is the or who is the first source of that information?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Probably the Ukrainian at check-point 2 who passed it on to the -- their commanding officer, who then passed it on to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And mechanically, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber what means this information or by what means this information was being communicated from the Ukrainian Company in Zepa up to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: The same type of radio that I mentioned earlier, HF, high-frequency, radio that the Ukrainians were using regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, is that any kind of special equipment, by the way, that HF equipment, is that newfangled in any way?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think it was standard issue in the Ukrainian army. It looked very old, but it was working. We were not using that kind of equipment any longer. It's something we had gotten rid of a few years prior at least in my army. We were using shorter range but more, I should say, efficient equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P00596 at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received, and I take the opportunity to say that the documents P584, 588, and 589 don't have a B/C/S translation. They will be marked pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions for you, Colonel. In your statement to the OTP many years ago, you discussed a meeting that you also testified about in the Popovic case that was held on 27 July 1995 between three civilian representatives from Zepa, in which Mladic was trying to get these men to sign an agreement. Do you remember that testimony, first of all, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you said at page 24 of that witness statement that General Smith told these individuals that they shouldn't sign because they were being fooled by Mladic, and you further added in the statement that they must have been afraid for their lives. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber, sir, based on your observations, your experience, why you made that statement, they must have been afraid for their lives.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, General Smith was not -- was not there initially when the meeting started. In fact, we had arrived, Colonel Soubirou who I accompanied who was to be in charge of all the UN troops because we had deployed more troops to Zepa to make sure that something like what happened -- had happened in Srebrenica not long before, that we could prevent it from happening in Zepa. And so we met there with Lieutenant-Colonel Germain who was a French legion officer. And at that time we heard that a meeting was going to occur between a Serb officer and three civilian leaders of the Bosniak in Zepa. So we got to where that meeting was supposed to be held and we said we wanted to attend. The man in charge who we didn't see at the time said, "Well, the Canadian can come with an interpreter." So I took a legionaire originally from Slovenia who could speak the language and I went to the table. And Mladic was sitting there. We waited for a while until at least two of the three Bosniaks arrived, and then the meeting started. Mladic wanted them to sign an agreement to basically leave the pocket, allow the military -- the few Bosniak military in there to disarm. And he was not too - how should I say? - not too subtle about what would happen to them if they did not sign. Shortly after General Smith arrived and he came -- he came directly to that meeting and intervened, and that's when he saw what General Mladic was attempting to get their agreement on. In there it required many guarantees by UNPROFOR, guarantees that UNPROFOR could not give. So he told those Bosniaks not to sign the agreement because if they were hoping for UNPROFOR to provide the guarantees that were stated in that agreement, Smith was telling them: We cannot provide those guarantees. So you're basically handing over your fate to the Serb general. But they signed it anyway because I guess it was better than their current stalemate and their current stalemate was they were encircled by the VRS, and the only end for them was to be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I want to show you last, Colonel, are some handwritten notes that you took on the 28th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could take a look at P00582, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance I'd like to hand up to you a copy that I pulled out from our evidence vault. I noticed as I was preparing for today that one of the pages was scanned improperly in our evidence unit and is therefore illegible both in our databases and unfortunately in e-court. So I've provided legible copies to the Defence and we have copies for the Trial Chamber. So I just want to make sure that we have a proper reading and understanding of this document from a legible copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did the Defence receive a copy as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did furnish copies to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you see what's on the screen and is it the same as what you've got in your hand, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, what are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm looking at a report that I wrote following the meeting between General Gobillard and General Tolimir at the Ukrainian check-point 2 in Zepa. The Ukrainian check-point 2 is basically the end of the road on top of the hill where there was a large parking area and a Ukrainian check-point. So on the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to the third page in the English version and the corresponding page in the B/C/S is page 2. And let's focus on paragraph 2 and pretty much the second half of the paragraph, if we could blow that up a little bit beginning where it says: "As for the Bosnian military ..." As about halfway, maybe two-thirds of the way down the page. Could I, Colonel, just ask you to read into the record this section that begins with: "As for the Bosnian military ..."

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: "As for the Bosnian military, it seems that they are ready and willing to drop their weapons and surrender provided they obtain firm guarantees for their safety from UNPROFOR. It was pointed out that UNPROFOR cannot provide these guarantees unless there is a prisoner of war exchange agreement at the airport. Tolimir offered the UN the opportunity to send vehicles to the hills to gather Bosnian civilian and military personnel."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's just stick with this passage first. Do you recall, sir, what the source of this information in this sentence "as for the Bosnian military, it seems that they are ready and willing to drop their weapons and surrender provided they obtain firm guarantees for their safety from UNPROFOR ..." where this information came from. Is this something that's being reported to you from General Tolimir, is this something you're observing yourself, or are you receiving this information from another source?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure where it's coming from. It may have been reported by General Tolimir, but it may also have come from General Gobillard who had driven to Zepa that day and I had just linked with him. I had been in Zepa already for a couple of days. And so he had access -- he had discussions about what had happened in Srebrenica and what was going on in Zepa. It may have come from him, but I'm not sure really.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And the next sentence where it says: "It was pointed out that UNPROFOR cannot provide these guarantees unless there is a POW exchange agreement at the airport ..." Who's doing the pointing out here, sir?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: It was General Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And now if we could go to the next page and this is the page where I think the e-court is illegible at the top. Can you just read into the record from the legible version what this top sentence says here that follows on what you finished reading from the prior page.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: "UNPROFOR officers concluded privately that this was not a good idea as long as there was not a global agreement," which the good idea was basically sending UN troops through the hills to gather whatever Bosniaks remain there and offer them a guarantee of personal security or safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you explain then what this means here, where you've written "UNPROFOR officers concluded privately that this was not a good idea as long as there was not a global agreement," can you just explain that for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, we were not about to help the VRS capture men between 18 and 55 and hand them over without having some firm guarantees of what would happen to them later on. So if there was a global prisoner of war exchange agreement, we could bring the Red Cross, we could provide security for these people until the proper exchange was made. If there was no such agreement, the risk was that at the time we didn't have enough troops to be able to do that right away -- and so the risk was we hand over these people to the VRS and they do to them like what they did to the people of Srebrenica a couple of weeks before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether at the time that this was going on, Colonel, the issue of the Serbs' failure to account for what happened to the missing men from Srebrenica contributed to the inability to come to a global agreement?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I must read that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's a terrible question. Let me ask it again, Colonel. Were you aware at the time whether or not the Serbs' inability to account for or explain what happened to the men from Srebrenica prevented the two parties from being able to come together to a global POW exchange agreement? Did you ever become aware of whether that became an obstacle to that agreement, the inability to account for those men from Srebrenica during those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, it is probably a likely explanation, but not a complete -- it does not explain everything. I believe that for the Serbs to move in and reduce those enclaves two and a half years after the start of the war was because they were beyond that now. They wanted to get rid of those problems, problems that they were not able to solve initially when they launched their operation towards Bosnia to capture the country because of resistance in those areas. Now they had decided that they had enough and they wanted to get rid of those enclaves. Of course, the UN interfered so it didn't go as planned. So I think that that's -- would be the main reason. They were beyond negotiating. They wanted to get rid of those enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Tolimir, you indicated you would need eight hours for cross-examination. If it is possible, we would appreciate if you could finish your cross-examination by the end of hearing tomorrow, taking into account that we -- I don't want to put any time pressure on you because you indicated you have lots of documents to show to the witness, but please proceed and start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Peace in this house and may God help all those present, including the witness. And I would like these proceedings to be completed not as I will but according to God's will. I do have one question. We announced ten hours that we would need for this witness, not eight. This is one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are perfectly right. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best. When I run out of questions, I'm not going to stretch out the time like -- in the way that I haven't been doing up to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct. Please proceed and put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fortin, I would like to wish you a good afternoon and wish you a pleasant stay in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief you said that you came to Bosnia in May 1995. You told this to Mr. Thayer. Can you please tell us how long you spent in Bosnia and were you always on the same duty, just like it says in your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I spent a year in Bosnia. I arrived in May 1995 and I left in May 1996; and, yes, I stayed in the same job, military assistant to the sector commander. However, when there was a transfer of authority to NATO, the sector became a brigade as part of a division. So most of the responsibilities we had at sector level towards the factions were taken over by this new higher level, which is the division level. But in my case, I remained military assistant to the French general in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted you to say that for the transcript. So up until the time the NATO forces came, you were the military assistant to the sector commander and that was General Gobillard; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That was General Gobillard until mid-August; he was then replaced by General Bachelet, another French officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain for the transcript when the duty was transferred and when you moved from UNPROFOR to your duties in NATO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, the transfer of authority to NATO occurred on the 20th of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch on your microphone, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And at that time from your duty as military assistant to the sector commander, you became the military assistant to the commander of the NATO brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's correct -- one of the NATO brigades because of course there were many more troops coming in at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During the examination-in-chief you said that the seat of the UNPROFOR command in 1995 was located in Zagreb. I would like to ask you this now: Do you know when did this command HQ move to Zagreb, the UNPROFOR HQ?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Actually, before events in Bosnia the mission in Croatia, the UN mission in Croatia, was called UNPROFOR. Eventually with the new mission in Bosnia, the mission headquarters in Zagreb was renamed headquarters UN PF, United Nations Protection Force. And the mission in Bosnia took the name UNPROFOR, with its headquarters commanded by General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell us whether you know that the UN mission first was located in Belgrade and then in Sarajevo, and only after that in Zagreb? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's probably before my time and I'm not aware of the -- what happened in the two or three years before I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you if you know that in 1991 the UN mission for the former Yugoslavia was first located in Belgrade. Are you aware of that or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I may have heard that, but no I was not aware of when exactly, what was the name of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This was an observer mission headed by General Walker who was a Prosecution witness in trials in this Tribunal. Are you aware that that mission was transferred from Belgrade to Sarajevo while the war was going on in Croatia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the mission was transferred to Zagreb immediately after the signing of the agreement in Croatia and that Bosnia was declared a risk -- high-risk zone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: When was that agreement signed that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an agreement that was signed between the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, if you recall - do you recall? - and Zagreb. Do you recall that agreement? And the UN mission that was implementing that agreement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that agreement. It was outside of my territory and we had pretty much enough to keep us busy in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that the federal government of Yugoslavia, before Yugoslavia broke apart in 1991, gave 300 vehicles to the UN mission from the federal government and they then went to Bosnia because they wanted the HQ to be in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that Bosnia was an oasis of peace for the United Nations while the conflict was raging in Croatia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware. And not knowing the full details, I was aware that Bosnia was a fairly safe for a while, and the reason I'm aware is a Canadian General, General Lewis MacKenzie who was the Chief of Staff of that UN mission at that time went to Sarajevo when things started to go sour, but I couldn't recall the exact dates, but I'm aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to tell us if on the basis of what the Canadian officers who were in that mission said, that Bosnia was declared a war zone overnight from a peaceful oasis once the conflict was finished in Croatia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about overnight. All I know from the Canadian perspective - and I was in Canada when this was happening - was that a Canadian unit who was part of the mission in Croatia drove all the way to Sarajevo because problems were starting to happen there and they needed a unit -- military forces to protect the airport. So that's how I know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know -- have you heard from the Canadian observers that the UNPROFOR observer mission forces in Bosnia used 300 Mercedes of the federal government of Yugoslavia while the war was raging in Croatia and that they didn't really need any combat vehicles in order to be able to implement their mission? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I was not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As a military expert and analyst, are you able to say why the UN forces and UN personnel immediately switched to the NATO contingent when the authority was transferred to that force? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean. Could you please rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were a military assistant at the UN -- UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb until the authority was transferred; is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was a military assistant in Sarajevo, not Zagreb, and I was there when the transfer of authority occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And since you said earlier that the transfer of authority took place in December after the signing of the Dayton Accords in 1995, did you immediately become an assistant but now in the NATO forces brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: In my case, yes, I did. And I see what you were asking earlier. For those countries member of NATO who were already providing troops to the UN, if their government agreed it was fairly simple to basically change hat from a blue hat to a green hat and remain with the new mission, new mission which also had new modes of operations and more means and a new mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it easy to make this change practically in the course of one night and one day? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, changing the hat was much faster than one night and one day, but changing the mandate was a bit longer than that. And the preparations occurred in the months before -- I mean, it did not start happening on the 20th of December. It started before with all sorts of planning. I remember the ARC commander, the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps who would command the NATO operation came to visit a couple of months before to start devising plans with his staff and to determine how that would happen. So we started before of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the commander of the Rapid Reaction Force. Was that the French General Soubirou? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, sir. You are confusing the Rapid Reaction Force that the French and British were putting together in late June 1995 and the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, NATO organisation, that eventually came and took command of the new UN mandated mission but executed by NATO troops in December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me. But before July 1995 was the commander of the Rapid Reaction Force in fact serving at the UNPROFOR headquarters in Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: The Rapid Reaction Force that the French and British put together before NATO got in the picture was in fact commanded by a former Sarajevo Sector commander, who had returned to France, rejoined his army, and now was coming back in this new capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the Rapid Reaction Force operated under the UN mandate in June 1995 when the commander returned from France to Bosnia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that honestly. That force was created by the French and the British. It would have had to be included eventually in the UN mandate, but how that came about was quite a bit above my pay grade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you mentioned the IFOR commander, General Layton Smith, do you know what post he occupied before coming to Bosnia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think you're talking of the American admiral but I'm not sure what job he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he become the IFOR commander and before that he commanded the south wing of NATO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in all the observer missions the observers were intelligence officers in the -- and they did their job in the countries of the former Yugoslavia where there was war going on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: What you can say that the nature of their job was gathering information, but I know for a fact that not very many, if any, were trained intelligence officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you in Bosnia or in NATO forces while the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was bombed and during the war in Kosovo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I was back in Canada at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you ever served in Macedonia or in Albania? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what mission General Walker, the American General Walker, had in Kosovo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I do not, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the observer missions in the territory of Serbia, the UN observer missions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: While I was deployed in Bosnia and Sarajevo from May 1995 to May 1996, as far as I know all the UN observers were deployed within Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm not aware of observers elsewhere or at other times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You have told us about the UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb. Did it have several sectors and who was stationed in Sector North in Croatia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: With the UNPF headquarters in Zagreb was commanding two theatres, basically Croatia and Bosnia, and I'm not aware of the forces that were in the northern sector. I'm aware of the Canadian contribution to that mission, which was in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear of Vukovar and Western Slavonia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I heard the names and I could probably find them fairly quickly on a map, but it was outside of my area. And believe me, we had quite enough work to keep us busy in Sarajevo without concerning ourselves -- well, I'm speaking for myself, but without concerning myself with what was going on elsewhere. Had it been an adjacent sector to Sector Sarajevo, perhaps I would have paid more attention because it was geographical adjacent but it was not the case. So I'm not aware of the situation in those sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I asked you this because I wanted to see whether you know all the UNPROFOR commanders from the period while you were -- or rather, when the UNPROFOR headquarters was moved to Zagreb. Because are you aware of the fact that UNPROFOR was also stationed in Western Slavonia and in Vukovar? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I know that there were UN troops there, but they were not under UNPROFOR at that time. They had renamed the mission, so there was a different mission in Croatia that was looking after those UN troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that all the staff -- all the personnel who were observers in Sector North under the command of General Walker, who was also in Sector North, had been transferred from Vukovar to Kosovo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that all the UNPROFOR and NATO operations followed after military missions that had been deployed in the territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you're asking, sir. If you could rephrase, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, for instance, the combat operations in Kosovo were preceded by the military mission by General Walker, and you probably know about Racak. He claimed that a crime had been committed there, and in the end it turned out that there had been no crime. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, Kosovo happened later, after I had returned to Canada and occupied other functions. All I know about General Walker is he, probably the same, commanded the Allied Reaction Corps that was deployed to Bosnia in December 1995. What he did after, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, is that perhaps a convenient time for our first break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for giving me very fair answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our first break now for technical reasons. We will have a shorter break because of the sitting time today, and we will resume ten minutes before 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Could we please see in the e-court Exhibit P582. This is the memorandum that we just had up on the screen, and can we show it both in the English and in the Serbian versions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, can I please ask you to tell us if you know that in all the areas where there was war in the former Yugoslavia, first you had the observer missions, then you had the UNPROFOR forces, then you had the rapid force -- reaction force, and then NATO forces. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it happened in all the missions, but yes that was generally the deployment that occurred in Bosnia and probably in Kosovo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We are looking at this memorandum of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show page 2 of the document. Thank you. Can we look at page 2. Thank you. Could we zoom in on page 2, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In answer to Mr. Thayer's question - this is transcript page 17, lines 18 to -- actually, lines 11 to 19, you said how General Smith said that the UNPROFOR could not extend the guarantees to the agreement offered by Mladic, which he wanted the representatives of Zepa to sign with him. Can you please tell us whether that was so. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I can certainly give you a partial answer. For a more complete answer, you would have to ask General Smith because he was commander of all the forces. But from my understanding, one, we did not have all the troops to be able to observe all Serbian or VRS activity while they were collecting these people in the Zepa enclave because it was a fairly large area; and two, we were not willing to let the VRS hold, especially the men of military age, knowing that many men of the same age taken in Srebrenica had been killed and not held as prisoners of war; and finally, there was no all-encompassing agreement to have an exchange of prisoners of war between Serbian and Bosniaks when this was all over. And I think this was General Smith's main point, but for a more complete answer you would have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this on the 25th of July? This is what you said on page 20, lines 11 to 18, that General Smith what I said he said just now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the exact date. I would have to look at the document to confirm, but it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see the memorandum in front of us, your memorandum. Can you remember when it was written and when you were in Zepa when Smith was in Zepa, if you look at the memorandum? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I think it was -- I wrote this late on the 28th of July, as I was -- as I returned to Sarajevo with General Gobillard at that time. But General Smith was there the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were not there when General Smith was there. You're giving us hearsay evidence here; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, no. No. In fact, when General Smith first arrived, I was in a meeting with General Mladic and the two or three Bosniak representatives of Zepa. And then General Smith arrived and I talked to him along with other people at that time. The next day is when I wrote this, after General Gobillard had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the date for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I think from memory that the meeting of -- with General Mladic was on the 27th, and that's when General Smith arrived. And the next day, the 28th, is when I linked up with General Gobillard; and after his meeting with you, I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us, please, when the evacuation actually started because you tell us that you could see them take their things out of the houses. Could you tell us who was doing that and when that happened.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: When I went down to Zepa, I believe it was the evening of the 27th, is when I saw that. But the evacuation had started a few days before. The questions being discussed there were the people that were left, and estimates varied about how many people were left and who those people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just perhaps to save some re-direct time because I may not have any to get Mr. Fortin home, if we could just clarify for the record when the General and Colonel Fortin are referring to "see them take their things out of the houses," what are we talking about? Just to clarify who we're talking about, taking what out of whose houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I went down to the village, I saw Serb soldiers taking fridge, cows, mattresses from Bosniak houses -- Bosniak people who had been evacuated or were in the process of being evacuated, loading that stuff into trucks for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And could you please state for the record what date that was and what date the agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the Muslims leave before this agreement was signed or what happened? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I believe that -- like I said earlier, when I went down was the evening of the 27th of July, that's when I saw those things. And the meeting I attended was prior to leaving check-point 2 and going down to the village, meeting where Mladic was trying to obtain the agreement of the Bosniak representative, which he eventually got. But I was not present when he eventually got it, but I believe it's the same day. The evacuation of the population had started happening before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be able to see it from other witnesses' statements and we will also look at the full text of the agreement on the disarming and evacuation, so we don't want to waste any time. But please tell me when you were the second time with Gobillard on the 28th there, were the Rapid Reaction Forces deployed at the check-point, the first check-point, at the road at Boksanica, where the meeting between Mladic and the Muslims was held?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No. The Rapid Reaction Force was not deployed to Zepa. There was a original Ukrainian Company and some Russian and French troops were sent, but not troops of the Rapid Reaction Force. And I make the distinction because the Rapid Reaction Force had all the heavy military hardware, whereas the UN troops who were deployed, they simply had their own rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Had the Rapid Reaction Force been already deployed in Bosnia by that time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Some elements. I don't remember the exact date of when they were complete on the ground, but some elements had been deployed as early as late June. But this did not happen overnight. It took quite some time to deploy all of the elements, but they were deploying in areas like Sarajevo and none were sent to the eastern enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo asked from UNPROFOR that the Rapid Reaction Force be deployed in Zepa and that they told the Muslims in Zepa to refuse signing the agreement because they had promises that the Rapid Reaction Force would be deployed there? Are you aware of that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I became aware that the Muslim government was making all kinds of demands, but I don't think they were ever promised that the Rapid Reaction Force would be deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the agreement was signed on the 24th of July --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, since the agreement was signed on the 24th of July - we have it here after all - and its implementation was delayed, was this in any way related to the arrival of the Rapid Reaction Force demanded by the Muslims? Could there be any link there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I don't see why because UNPROFOR was not a party to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell us whether the Rapid Reaction Force was an integral part of UNPROFOR and what kind of mandate it had, if you know? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: It was not quite an integral part of UNPROFOR. It was given eventually, but I'm not sure when, under command of commander UNPROFOR, but it had a separate command structure. I'm not sure who else they reported to, so I'm not very familiar with the chain of command of the Rapid Reaction Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's enough. There's no need for us to burden the Trial Chamber any longer about this issue, why the implementation of the agreement was delayed by four days. Now, Mr. Thayer asked you here about Tolimir's role when he offered the possibility that the vehicles be sent into the mountains to pick up Muslim civilians and military personnel. Now, was this conveyed to you or is it something that you heard? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I was there when you had the discussion with General Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us what I offered to Gobillard, because in the sentence quoted by the Prosecutor it has not been specified and after all I'm on trial here for some of the statements that I allegedly made. So could you please tell the Trial Chamber what is it that I offered General Gobillard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's in the memorandum. From memory, you were offering the UN to go and pick up those remaining people in the enclave, which was the best way for UNPROFOR to ensure the security of those people. As I mentioned earlier, we didn't have the means to do that, considering that it was a wide area, it was a very hilly area, the Bosniaks' military remnants which were those concerning you mostly had been hiding in that area for a long time, and that would have been an endeavour with no end. We didn't have the means to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So those were soldiers of the Zepa Brigade who refused to be disarmed in accordance with the agreement or are we talking about civilians here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, we thought at the time that there were elements of both remaining in Zepa, some civilians and some members of the Zepa Brigade which were not ready to give up. You didn't think so. You thought that only military from the Zepa Brigade remained in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to look at paragraph 6 of your memorandum where Tolimir is mentioned again and to explain to us -- well, to give us some additional explanations. I will ask you questions after you've read the document. Thank you. Now that you've read it my question to you would be: Did this happen on the 28th in the conversation between myself and General Gobillard? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And on the 28th did General Gobillard ask me if Avdo Palic had been killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's what it says. If he knew if it was true that he had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know by any chance when Avdo Palic was killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the Trial Chamber will definitely be able to determine that, and if you know he had not been killed at the time and I said what I knew at the time. It was probably part of the propaganda because by that time -- at that time he was not dead yet. Now I would like us to look at the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness statement provided to the Prosecution on the 19th, 20th, 21st, and 22nd of November, 1997. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the statement to come up on our screens, can you please tell us whether you gave this statement in the course of a trial on the 19th, 20th, 21st, and 22nd of November, 1997, when you came here to testify at a trial?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No. A court lawyer came to Canada to take that statement from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please look at 1D206, that's the number of the statement, because we will now be focusing on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see the front page in English, and I can see it in my mother tongue. Is this the statement that you gave and that you signed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yeah, it's that first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2 of this statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to look at paragraph 4 of this statement in the English language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it correct that I asked you whether you had transferred from UNPROFOR forces to the multi-national division of IFOR, NATO, immediately and that this was true both for you and for your superior commander, General Zeller, is that correct because this is what you state in your statement. So could you please confirm for the record.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like us to look at page 3 of the statement in Serbian and I assume it's the same in English, but let us have a look and then we'll check. Thank you. Now, in the first paragraph of this page it says that you did all operative work in this UNPROFOR unit and later on in the IFOR unit as the military assistant. Is that correct or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, it basically says that I kept the same job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 2 the Rapid Reaction Forces are referred to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My question was whether the Rapid Reaction Forces command was in Kiseljak, as it is written here in this paragraph, number 4 in the witness's statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as you can see, that's what it says, headquarters in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 3 of the statement now, please, and can we look at the last paragraph on that page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You can see the last sentence. It says that: "Sector Sarajevo was headquartered in the PTT building. This is the post office, telephone, and telegraph building. When I talk of my duties initially in May 1995, the sector commander was General Herve Gobillard. He was posted back to France" -- page 4, please, can we look at page 4, "on the 12th of August, 1995. Thank you. This is on page 4. I hope you're able to follow. "He was replaced by General Jean-Rene Bachelet on the 9th of August, 1995. General Bachelet was replaced in early December 1995 by General Louis Zeller, who I mentioned above. General Zeller arrived on December 11. All the sector commanders I served under were French. The nature of my job as military assistant only changed under General Zeller, as the mandate of the multi-national forces serving in the former Yugoslavia had changed completely with the transfer of authority. Otherwise, my duties and responsibilities remained the same, but with Bachelet there were more occasions when we were doing things that the UN and he wanted to let the world see. For instance, when we were opening the highway into Sarajevo, we had a press conference on the scene. I would translate for Bachelet on those occasions." My question is: Can you please tell me whether all these French commanders from UNPROFOR later remained in the IFOR forces on the same posts and on the same duties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: In fact, General Gobillard returned home to France after one year in Sarajevo as commander of Sector Sarajevo in August 1995. General Bachelet also returned to France after a shorter period. He was there from August to early December, but he returned to France to assume other duties. General Zeller, who was in charge as of early December and therefore was in charge during the transfer of authority on the 20th of December remained as commander of the Sarajevo Brigade.
