But as I alluded to earlier, when Mr. Thayer was questioning me, for us at sector level, we now became brigade -- a NATO brigade and that changed the nature of our responsibilities because it was a new level of command that was created. Above us, the new level was the division, divisional level, which is higher than brigade. The divisional level assumed all the duties that the sector was performing during the UNPROFOR mandate. So the division -- the new divisional level was assuming those duties within the NATO deployment. So the brigade lost a lot of -- we were not responsible any longer for contacts with the corps, for example, either Bosniak or Serb, VRS, corps. We lost that responsibility to the division. So that's what I'm saying in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show page 5 of the statement to the witness, please, paragraph 4 and can we zoom in on that text, please, thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see this paragraph now, paragraph 4, which says: "There were three French Battalions in Sarajevo. French Battalion 2 was at the airport. Their duties were to protect the airport, run Bosnian convoys across the airport, and later run a two-way crossing for Bosnian and Serb populations." Thank you. End of quote. My question is: Was this true during the UNPROFOR mandate in Bosnia and are you able to tell us what Bosnian convoys did you run across the airport? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Okay. Bosnian convoys across the airport occurred before I arrived. As I was saying earlier, when I landed on May 15th, it was the second or third day of the Bosniak offensive to break out of Sarajevo and the airport was closed because there was firing on both sides and there were no more convoys. My understanding is that those convoys were to bring in food to the population of Sarajevo based on prior agreements between the two factions. Of course that agreement went out the door when the fighting resumed on May 12th, 13th, or 14th, 1995, so those are the convoys I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what UNPROFOR did in order to stop the fighting by the Muslims in their attacks on Ilidza on the 12th, 13th, and 14th of May? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any intervention that I was a part of, but I know that the sector headquarters staff were in -- having meetings with the Bosniak corps in Sarajevo and probably sending protest letters. But I was brand new so I didn't know everything that was going on at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to explain to the Trial Chamber whether Sarajevo was a protected area when you got there in May and was it able to carry out offensive actions against the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was supposed to be protected area, but no side, yours or theirs, was respecting the prior agreements. Agreements concerning weapon collection points, for example, were not respected. So it was not much of a protected area for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And does that justify the Muslims' attack on Serbs in that period when you just arrived?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, we have to look at the bigger situation, and the bigger situation is the VRS tried to capture the whole of Bosnia initially. They were not able to capture Sarajevo and the three eastern enclaves, so they were surrounding these areas, choking them, and people were starving. So is it justified that the Bosniaks were trying to break out so that they could obtain resupply based on their own wishes as opposed to the VRS deciding what goes in and what not? That's debatable I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this opinion shared by UNPROFOR unit commands, just like the one that you stated for us today in this courtroom? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: What I have just stated is Fortin's opinion, my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at page 7 of your statement now, please, lines 1, 2, and 3. Thank you. We can see that it's the first paragraph. You say: "What I did write was an ultimatum that we sent to return the weapons that were compiled or we would bomb them. We did not bomb them and they were not returned."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not find the place in the statement in the original text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm repeating my question. Did this happen at the time when the Muslims were conducting attacks on Serbian positions? Was that the period when you were collecting the weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I will read the text first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's on a different page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, just so we have a clear record later on in case this particular document isn't tendered or for any other reason. I believe that the portion that General Tolimir's referring to is on page 7, it's the last sentence of the second full paragraph on 0055-5111: "For instance, around May 20th, 1995, when the Bosnian Serbs started using weapons around the WCPs, we wrote letters. One that I wrote was an ultimatum that we gave them to return weapons to the WCPs or that we would bomb. They did not, and we bombed." I think that's slightly different as was appeared in the transcript a few moments ago. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to have that on the screen. It should be perhaps on the next page. Are we on page 7?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it here. It's below the bold title "Records," the second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- last few sentences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Now your question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My question was in his statement did the witness write: "The one that I wrote was an ultimatum that we gave to them to return weapons to the weapons collection points or that we would bomb. They did not and we bombed." Thank you. I wanted the witness to read that so that I could put a question to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He did and now you should put a question. [Overlapping speakers] repetition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you state this in your statement, since Mr. Thayer said that there was a difference in the statement. Does the same thing -- does your statement say the same thing in English? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if there's a -- if there's a translation problem, but I understand what I wrote on the English side, and that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you write an ultimatum to the Serbs, that they should return weapons to the weapons collection points, and if not they would be bombed; and since they did not return the weapons, they were bombed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's correct. I wrote the statement and the results are as laid out in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the Serbs were bombed because they took their weapons in self-defence, but the Muslims were not even though they attacked them? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, the problem here is the type of weapons. Weapons collection points were created to store heavy weapons. Heavy weapons means heavy mortars, not 82-millimetre or less but bigger; artillery; tanks and other vehicles of the sort. The Bosniaks have very little of that type of equipment. There was a Bosniak weapon collection point in Sarajevo, but they didn't have all the heavy equipment because that heavy equipment was seized by the VRS, it was the former Yugoslav Army equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Can you tell us if UNPROFOR tolerated infantry attacks from the Muslims against the Serbs and punished the Serbs for each violation of the agreement on the collection of heavy weaponry at certain check-points that were under UNPROFOR control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I would put it that way, but the UN was sent to intervene to protect population in those enclaves, Sarajevo included, that could not be taken militarily initially in the war by the VRS. So that's the whole point of the UN deployment, was to protect those populations. And since the VRS was encircling the city and strangling it, preventing food from coming in, yes, the Bosniaks were attempting to break out while the UN was attempting to negotiate more food and UN convoys coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell this Trial Chamber that is presiding in this case whether these weapons were in the hands of the Serbs when you sent the ultimatum and were these weapons always weapons that belonged to the Serbs other than they had to be at these check-points that under -- that were under your supervision? Did they take something that was already theirs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, those are former Yugoslav Army weapons taken by the VRS early in the war. And, yes, following an agreement with UNPROFOR they - the Serbs - had agreed to put those weapons in weapons collection points. Again, I remind that those are heavy weapons, artillery, tanks, and things like that; and those are the weapons that were taken from the weapon collection points, breaking the agreement, and used to fire on Sarajevo, a starving city at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it say in the agreement that the weapons can be used in self-defence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir, the exact details of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the sentence that's one sentence below this one that you've just read. It's -- you say: "I believe General Smith was doing the same things at his level. We always discussed sending an ultimatum to the Bosnian Serbs with him, of course, prior to doing so." Thank you. So did you say that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we normally did. Like I said earlier, we were operating at the corps level. General Smith was operating at army Main Staff level. Usually we agreed on something before we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you say if an ultimatum issued by you, your command, or General Smith was ever -- if any such ultimatums threatening bombing was ever sent to Muslims? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I don't recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you go on to say in your statement when you speak about sniping in that chapter, can you tell us whether Muslims had snipers in Sarajevo, yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I don't know if they had snipers in the same -- in the same way, because from -- however, as I say, I was fired at by the Muslims as well as the Serbs, but they were not snipers. They were firing from the window of a basement right near the street where I was driving by. But I don't think they had snipers in the same way that sniping was coming from Serb hill Grbavica, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it something that you think or are you sure about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please look at the fifth passage in your statement where General Crouch is mentioned. You say he came in before he took up his post in IFOR. Why did he come to Sarajevo, in what capacity, when UNPROFOR was deployed there?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Like I said earlier, the deployment of NATO troops -- or planning for the deployment of NATO troops started before the actual date of transfer of authority. And as soon as the Dayton Accords was signed, we started receiving reconnaissance missions from NATO units who would -- who were designated to start preparing for deployment. And I believe General Crouch was a senior member of the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, and he was coming in such a reconnaissance to look at the terrain, to look at the situation, to look at where they could put additional troops that were coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us whether that corps had a mandate within UNPROFOR or NATO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, that corps took command as IFOR as of December 20th, so it had no mandate under UNPROFOR. All it had was following the Dayton Accords reconnaissance started by these people to see where they would bring their people and be ready to take command on the 20th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You say here in line 8, paragraph 5: "I was there with General Bachelet," that's your commanding officer, "and General Crouch, even before Crouch took up duties as part of IFOR." Now, my question is: Can you tell us the time-period so that we can have it on the record because you're talking about Dayton Peace Accords and it did happen before that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, I don't see that text on the e-court, but what I'm saying is that you are a trained military officer, you know how to conduct -- bring in reinforcements or conduct relief in place. These things don't happen overnight, especially talking about thousands of troops with heavy equipment. So as soon as there was an accord that NATO would take-over the UN mission, these things, preparations, started happening and that's one example of that. Even before that, officers from UNPROFOR-contributing nations could come and visit their troops and look at the terrain and see in what conditions their soldiers were operating. So these kinds of visits were not out of the ordinary. But in this particular case, it was planning for the upcoming NATO deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were unable to find it in the English text. Could you please look at line 3 here in the English version, there's mention here of General Crouch. So please look at it because I would like to ask you some additional questions in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you remember if it was in December or before December? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly when, but it was close to December because we had access to Grbavica, where we could not go before. And this is on -- Grbavica is a portion of the city that was held by the Serbs, and we could even go and visit the underground system that had been developed for people to move covertly from one firing position to the next. And I mention that because from a military -- from a soldier's point of view, it was well done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in order to determine the time-frame, was that after the first and the second air-strikes on the Republika Srpska army positions in Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: It was well after.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you tell us the reconnaissance mission and the deployment of those large units with heavy weapons before the Dayton Peace Agreement, could it have affected the outcome of the Dayton negotiations and, in fact, the Dayton Peace Agreement itself? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: It did not occur -- deployment did not occur before the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And Crouch's reconnaissance mission, did it take place before the Dayton Agreement? Thank you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. There were visits by staff officers from the UN-contributing nations before that, but planning visits for the deployment did not occur before Dayton, but Dayton was signed before the transfer of authority date. So there was some time in between to do those reconnaissance and planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us if you know that whether General Crouch was deployed in Albania and Macedonia during the war in Kosovo, yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No idea, sir. I would not even recognise the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us what post he held in Bosnia after the Dayton Peace Agreement. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I don't know either, sir. I believe he [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] was part of the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, the designated NATO land unit that was deploying, but I don't know any more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could he have been the chief of the American delta teams, since he went there to observe the anti-sniping fighting against -- in Sarajevo that was conducted by the French Battalion, as you say here in line 3 of paragraph 5 here?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, like I said I don't remember much about the man, but I don't think so. Delta teams are not commanded by generals, they're commanded by captains and majors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just a correction for the record at page 56, line 14 for us, I know Your Honours may have a different line cite, it's the answer that begins with "I wouldn't know, the next sentence starts with "I was part of the Allied Reaction Corps NATO-designated land unit that was deploying, but I don't know any more precisely." I'm not sure that that reflects the witness's answer properly, if we could just get a clarification for that. That was an answer to a question about this General Crouch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be "he was part."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That clarifies the situation. Mr. Tolimir, I think this is perhaps a convenient time for the second break. It will be a shorter one as well, and we will resume at quarter past 6.00. Thank you very much. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like the witness to be shown page 9 of this statement, the one that we see here. The chapter is "Major Events." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, please look at paragraph 4 here. You say: "I arrived in Sarajevo during the course of the second or third day of the Bosnian offensive to try and break out of the city." Do you see that in the English language?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Not yet, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on page 10, the second paragraph, in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So let me repeat. "I arrived in Sarajevo during the course of the second or third day of the Bosnian offensive to try and break out of the city. Most of the shelling during those few days was in the southern part of the city and at Debelo Brdo. The sector had two observation posts which were right in the middle of this offensive and being pounded by mortars, artillery, and rifle grenades from both sides. After some time, the Bosnian side moved their offensive to another location, Nedzarici. For a period of about two weeks, from late May until early June, they were attacking every morning to try and break out towards Ilidza. They were never able to do so." Did I quote you properly here and did this Muslim attack in fact take about 15 days, as you say here?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we move on to the next paragraph which reads as follows: "In response to the Bosnian attack, the Bosnian Serbs started to fire their weapons which had been gathered in the weapons collection points. The sector issued an ultimatum to the Bosnian Serbs to stop firing and to return their weapons to the points by noon on May 25th, 1995, or risk air-strikes. They failed to do so and there was an air-strike on May the 25th. That evening, however, the Bosnian Serbs continued to fire from three firing positions -- or rather weapons collection points. And as a consequence, a second air-strike took place during the morning of May 26th, 1995. Before the end of the morning, the sector and BH command were already receiving reports that UNMOs had been taken hostage in Pale." Thank you. Did I read your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of reading out those two passages, my question is the following: Were Bosnian Serbs punished because they had taken the weapons, heavy weapons, out of the collection points in self-defence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, they were punished because they took the heavy -- heavy weapons out of the collection points, type of heavy weapons that the other side did not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So Muslims were allowed to attack Serb positions every morning during the 15 days and those positions were then defended using those heavy weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: And your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So did UNPROFOR allow the Muslims to attack during the 15 days Serbs every morning with impunity and then punished the Serbs the moment they started defending themselves? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, as you know, the UN was deployed to keep things under control, prevent any attack, if possible, while negotiations at higher level tried to reach a solution. The Bosniaks, however, as I said earlier were home in Sarajevo in a city that had been surrounded for years and a city was starving because food was not coming in as much as was necessary. I should point out that initially - and perhaps my figures are off - but the point here, initially Sarajevo had about 350.000 people. At that point there were 420.000 people and not enough food going in. Additionally, the Bosniaks were intertwined with their own population, which was not the case of the surrounding VRS. So we could not bomb the Bosniaks, as is being alluded to here. And of course whenever the Bosniaks did that, they broke the peace, they broke the calm situation which we were there to prevent but we could not prevent it. We didn't have the means to be able to stop everything and we could not -- certainly not prevent it with air-strikes because that would have meant bombarding civilian populations in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did Muslims have a circle around the Sarajevo Serb positions at Igman and other positions that dominated Serb positions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't think any of the positions the Bosniaks held around Sarajevo were dominating, but I'm willing to admit that there were a few spots where it was. But as I said, they had very few heavy weapons. And Igman, perhaps looking at the map, it's higher but it's quite a distance to be able to bring any effective fire; it's too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You covered Sarajevo very well with your points, as you've told us. And now at page 10, could we please move to page 10 in the Serbian version. You speak about the so-called hostage crisis. You know what I want to ask you about so I don't have to read out all the paragraphs. You speak about how after the air-strikes Serbs took UNPROFOR soldiers hostage. That's what you say in paragraphs 1 through 6 on page 10, and this extends in fact all the way down to the end of this page, where you speak about 364 UNPROFOR staff who were taken hostage or detained in some other way; am I right?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I don't see the -- all the information, but the beginning is on the page that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Unfortunately, I don't speak English so I can't assist you, but that's what it says here. It's the whole of page 10 in the Serbian language is devoted to the hostage crisis that occurred after the government seat at Pale and the factory were bombed. You speak about three French combat vehicles that were moved out and you speak about the Ukrainians who had been captured the day before were taken towards Pale by bus, and then you say that the soldiers were chained to locations that were possible air-strike targets. Is that what it says in your statement?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Okay, it's coming up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just going to suggest moving to page 11, which we have now done, to help the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But yes, what you're reading is correct. This is what -- part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have not told you yet that in your statement you also speak about the -- when UNPROFOR moved from -- was transferred from the -- when the Vrbanja bridge was transferred from UNPROFOR hands to Bosnian Serb hands and back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, yes, but "transferred back" was -- fighting occurred between UNPROFOR and the VRS in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And you say that there were casualties on both sides in the fighting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's correct, and I could add that there was probably casualties on the Bosniak side as well because we -- when we -- French troops re-took the OP at Vrbanja bridge, they were in sight of Bosniak positions as well. And we did not trust that the Bosniaks would remain quiet in that counter-attack. So they received some fire as well from the French troops attacking to re-take that bridge or that observation post that was taken by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have approval from the UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb to use force to re-take Vrbanja Most, bridge?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if they were informed before the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement you then say that you were always warned by Zagreb not to deal with such crises by force, not to use weapons?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, you have to point out where I say this, but as a general rule proportionality was a UN principle. If you're fired on, you respond with a weapon of similar type.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Who opened fire first, was it UNPROFOR at the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska or did the army fire at UNPROFOR first? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about two incidents here. The VRS took the observation post from the French. I'm not sure if there was much fighting at that time because the post was taken at night by a Serbian soldier dressed in French uniforms. They had kept those uniforms when they had captured I don't know how many French soldiers, but more than a hundred. And some Serb soldiers spoke French, so they approached at night and they took the post and captured the soldiers, soldiers who would later be put on display near the bridge with an officer pointing his gun at the head of a man saying stop air-strikes or we kill this man. So that's the first incident. The next day UNPROFOR French troops re-took the bridge and of course over -- during the night the Serbs had reinforced their position with troops. So force was used right from the start to re-take that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was after the 26th and the 25th when you carried out the first and the second air-strike. Do you know what was the target of the bombing on those occasions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't know what the targets were. Perhaps I knew then, but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I remind you, do you recall that a barracks in Pale, a factory in Pale, and the government building of the Government of Republika Srpska was also bombed in Pale at that occasion, do you remember that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I cannot confirm that either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you remember if the Serbs killed any French soldiers when they took the Vrbanja bridge? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: When they initially took the bridge at night, I don't think they killed any French soldiers. In the subsequent French attack, there were two French soldiers killed and 17 wounded I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So in the first attack the Serbs didn't kill anyone, they just captured some people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, that's correct. They captured the observation post and the people, the French soldiers, it contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And when the French UNPROFOR took that check-point under its control with weapons, then there was some shooting and some people were killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you try to return the observation post through negotiations, and in that way, through negotiations, prevent the killing of any French or Serb soldiers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That may have been, but I don't know. That was a decision by the French commander and I was not privy to everything but -- so I don't know if there was an attempt to negotiate before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the UNPROFOR also keep a certain number of soldiers as prisoners, the soldiers who had originally captured that check-point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I think there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Did you treat them as prisoners of war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I really don't know about the procedure exactly that followed. They were taken by the French and they were not exactly prisoners of war because this is -- was a UN mission. So it became a French thing, which I don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Serbs capture a number of the French and were they considered prisoners of war and did they have specific status too? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, yes. As I said earlier, when the Serbs initially took the observation point -- the observation post at the bridge, they also took the French people. I think there were 11 of them. How they were designated, what type of prisoner, I don't know. I know, however, that some of these soldiers were taken to the bridge and was shown on Serb TV. They were threatened with a handgun, showing us and the world that if NATO did not stop its bombing on the Serbs, that the French soldier would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these soldiers exchanged, those 11 and the four who had been captured by the Serbs on the Vrbanja bridge? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I know that eventually yes, but the four Serb soldiers were returned and the 11 French soldiers I think eventually returned the same way that other UN hostages were returned, through Belgrade. But I'm not sure in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the fifth paragraph on page 11 in the Serbian, and that is probably on page 12 in the English, you say how you met Indjic and Lugonja in order to exchange the French hostages they had and to return to you the hostages that you had. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I don't -- pardon me. I don't see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read it to you -- well, I don't know English. I'm reading the first, second, third, fourth, fifth paragraph, 11th page in the Serbian, where you say: "People were actually freed that night, but towards Belgrade, by the time the prisoners had made the route from Belgrade to Zagreb, Split, and Sarajevo, it was already June 5th. They had to walk down Mount Igman. There were trucks waiting for them at the bottom of Igman. From there, the men were tracked through Butmir to the airport. The general and I as well as a large number of other people were waiting for them." You waiting for those soldiers. Was that a result of those -- was that a result of that meeting you had with Colonel Meille -- actually that Colonel Meille had with Lugonja and Indjic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, they just brought up the page. Let me have a look. I'm not sure if they are the same hostages, the Vrbanja bridge hostages that we are talking about here, because there was in total close to 400 UN hostages at one point, and we're talking about 120 of them returning that way -- that particular night. Did that include the people from Vrbanja bridge, I have no idea, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And you are actually saying that this was after the meeting with Indjic and Lugonja. In one part of the statement, if you recall, you say that Indjic was not able to make the decision. Do you remember that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that but I believe that, yes, Indjic was not able to make that kind of decision. That would have to be made at a higher level because he was a lieutenant-colonel liaison officer for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Your liaison officers, were they able to make decisions that were opposite from the decisions made by your commanders? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: They'd better not if they want to keep their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you this in order to be fair to Indjic because he was just a liaison officer, not a commanding officer or someone who can decide on any matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And now your question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was Indjic a liaison officer who would convey what was ordered to him by his commander in Sector Sarajevo in the same way that you had liaison officers in your sector, or was he somebody who had the power to make decisions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the witness answered this question already on the last lines of page 66.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If he replied, I thank him. I didn't hear that answer. I didn't register it, so that is why I repeated the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He said that would have to be made at a higher level because he was a lieutenant-colonel liaison officer for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to UNPROFOR. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is a fair answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us whether you had civilian affairs officers from the International Red Cross or any other organisation that went together with the military in any kind of task that they were carrying out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, anything that concerned prisoners we would certainly involve the International Committee of the Red Cross, and I believe they were involved concerning the four Serb prisoners taken at Vrbanja bridge. And I believe they were also involved by UN prisoners coming back to us from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you think or were you sure that the prisoners held by UNPROFOR were reported to the International Red Cross? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I am sure that they were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to move to another topic now. You're talking about the road via Mount Igman that led to Sarajevo airport through which the Muslims and UNPROFOR received their supplies. Did I interpret this part of your statement correctly, and I think it's not necessary then for me to read from your statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Muslims prevent you from carrying out transport during the day, from using that road via Mount Igman that led to Sarajevo, did the Muslims prevent you from using that road during day-time? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, they did add difficulties at times. Sometimes we could use it freely; other times it was just too many people using that road and it was a very low capacity -- basically initially a mountain road made for mules, not for heavy trucks. But the alternative was to use the traditional road, the sierra road, which the Serbs would not allow us to use or would not grant proper freedom of movement to use. So that put the UN in a dilemma of using a road where we had more freedom of movement but with little capacity and with the ensuing consequences that the Serb thought that we were collaborating with the Bosniak on Igman, where in fact we were trying to feed ourselves and feed the city by bringing UNHCR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this crisis something that occurred during the hostage crisis and after the bombing, this crisis that put an end to the use of the Kiseljak road? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I believe so. It was shortly after that it was getting more difficult to bring food and other resources for the UN into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to read something to you and you can just listen carefully if you cannot find it. This is on page 14, first, second, third, fourth paragraph, I'm going to read from the beginning. I think in your copy it's probably on page 15. "Later on Colonel Meille briefed the general as to what he had been told by the 1st Corps where the points agreed upon during the meeting between Nicolai and Muratovic. That movement on the Igman road at night was reserved for the Bosnians and during the day for UNPROFOR, that Bosnians were to have total freedom of movement in the demilitarised zone and that the upkeep of the Igman road was the responsibility of Sector Sarajevo. Of course these points had been discussed but were not resolved in the manner reported by the 1st Corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We see it now on the screen in the English version, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what I have read to you and what you see in this paragraph, 4, can I put a question to you now? And the question is: Did the Muslims stop you from moving along the Igman road by day, the road that passed through the DMZ, which the Serbs then restored once they allowed the UN to take Igman?

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand, but if you refer to the paragraph that you just read it says there that of course these points had been discussed but were not resolved in the manner report by the 1st Corps. Although we felt we had little option but to use Igman road at the time because we were prevented by the Serbs from using better roads. The Bosniaks were not making it easy for us either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like you to look at the fourth paragraph in English, line 4, where it says that the Bosnians were to have total freedom of movement in the DMZ and that the upkeep of the Igman road was the responsibility of Sector Sarajevo." Is that what you stated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, yes. And that's exactly the point I made. The Bosnians reported to us that that was the agreement between Muratovic and General Nicolai, but it was not the agreement between Muratovic and Nicolai. And as I said, they were not making it easy for us either, and Mr. Muratovic liked to put us in a bad situation like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my question based on what you say, based on what I read, is the following: Did the Muslims prohibit you from moving through the demilitarised zone at Igman? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, they did not, but they did not make it easy to move through. There were agreements, for example, that we use it by day. But by day we were being fired on by the Serbs at the bottom of the hill and they were using it by night. But as you probably know better than me, the top of Mount Igman is not paved with multi-lane highways. They're all very low-capacity roads and it very quickly turned into traffic jams everywhere along the road between Tarcin and the actual hill to come down in the valley near the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So were you prohibited from using that road through the demilitarised zone at night, yes or no? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: We had agreed to put most of our traffic through during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I will have to read out the paragraph 5 just below paragraph 4. So I'm reading line 4 where you say: "Following the meeting, Meille learned that a UNHCR convoy which had come down the Igman route that night had been detained at the airport and that the DMZ was closed by the Bosnians. At the time we were attempting to resupply both Sarajevo and ourselves and trying to obtain more routes from the Serbs." Is this what you stated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, and I might add the next sentence: "Meanwhile, the Serbs perceived our use of the Igman route as co-operating with their enemy. A lot of the obstruction the Bosnians created only served to reinforce that perception and make our task difficult." I said that a little earlier, and I also said that generally we had more freedom of movement there than anywhere else, but the Bosniaks were not always making it easy for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the basis of what I've just read out to you, does it not follow that the Bosnians closed down the DMZ? Is this what you stated? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: They did not closing down. In fact, you read the statement yourself from Colonel Meille that he's trying to make the point to them that we have complete access to the DMZ. But in the reality, it was not happening -- or it was not always happening as we would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Why did they then force you to move by day while they used it by night? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's what I said. That was the agreement. As Colonel Meille pointed out in discussions with the Bosniaks, we have -- we want and we should have complete freedom of movement over Igman, but we can negotiate with the 1st Corps the traffic flow. And generally we took the road by day, they by night -- they did by night, but not always. Because we wanted to maintain freedom of movement, so using that road as much as we wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was the DMZ handed over to you as UNPROFOR once the Republika Srpska army withdrew from those positions on Mount Igman and was it the situation then that the Muslims exerted greater control of the road than UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say they exerted greater control, but it was the only route in and out, both for UNPROFOR and for the Bosniaks. And it was the only route in and out - the airport was not functioning at that time - to bring any food in, including food for UNPROFOR because at that time we didn't have much to eat either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If that road was used only by humanitarian convoys with food, why then would Muslims prohibit you from using that road to supply the population in Sarajevo? Did they use it for military purposes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Yes, they did. And I said it was a very low-capacity road so everything was competing for very little capacity. All of those issues, Bosniak military issues, UNPROFOR resupply, and mainly the largest quantities of anything that was brought in was food for the population, UNHCR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did -- were Muslims ever punished because they had taken control over the roads and the demilitarised zone on Mount Igman? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: There were a lot of discussions, a lot of unhappiness - I shall put it that way - on the part of UNPROFOR. But punishing the Muslims, with air-strikes is probably what you're alluding to, would have meant punishing ourselves as well because we were basically occupying the same ground, whether in the city or on the very low-capacity road over Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you punish only the Serbs with air-strikes when we're talking about the warring sides in the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia or Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: As far as I recall, sir, yes we punished only the Serbs, considered as the aggressor in this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did UNPROFOR consider the Serbs as aggressors in this war? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: That's what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you be an aggressor in Canada, in your own home? Did those Serbs come from somewhere else, from some other state, or were they born there, in the territory where the war was going on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, if I take all the weapons of my army and encircle a city and starve it, I certainly am the aggressor even if I'm born in that country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that in Sarajevo there were heavy weapons, howitzers, and tanks in all -- that were left behind by the JNA in all the barracks, Jusuf Dzonlic, Marsal Tito, and in all the barracks, wherever there were heavy weapons in Sarajevo they were left behind? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: I saw those things you mentioned on a road outside near Stup and they had been destroyed very early in the war, and the bodies were still there two years later along with non-functioning tanks with big holes in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And where were the howitzers and the cannons that they kept, the ones that were in the barracks because the JNA as it withdrew did not take those weapons with it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: Well, as I say, I believe a lot of it was destroyed in the initial fighting. When the Serbs were trying to Sarajevo, the Bosniaks defended with those weapons that remained there. Whatever was left, was not -- there were not very many heavy weapons, like I said. All I personally saw were small calibre mortars, 82-millimetre, RPGs, and rifles and machine-guns, 14.5 machine-guns and that type of weapons. I didn't see any artillery, although there might have been, and certainly no tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that by the 15th of May until the JNA was still in Bosnia, that the Bosnian Presidency invited all the Muslims to leave the JNA ranks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LOUIS FORTIN
utterances.text: No, sir, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are running out of time. We have reached the 7.00 limit. We must break now and continue tomorrow morning. Before we do that, just for the record some very small corrections. The document P515 was only marked for identification pending translation. We have discovered that this was a mistake. We have a translation so that this is admitted as P515.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: On line 13 it should read -- yes, thank you. And the Prosecution has indicated that they don't want to attach translations for the notebooks we have seen. We have seen six of them admitted pending translation and only marked for identification. As it is not necessary to have translations, these will be received as P438, P439, P440, tendered with the Witness PW-033 and P508, P515 [sic], and P516 tendered with Witness PW-035. That's a clarification for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Another correction, please, on line 21 it should read P514 instead of P515. I think now we have it. Sir, thank you for your attendance today. We have to continue tomorrow --
